extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in communications/media studies interested in humor, persuasion, and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A content-analytic case study of a single stand-up comedian (Hannibal Buress) to identify which classical theories of humor and which persuasive techniques his material uses, and how sociopolitical themes appear across his work. The study codes jokes by humor-theory, persuasive strategy, and thematic content, then reports counts/percentages and temporal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief theory suggests humor is drawn from the build-up and release of tension, often as a defense mechanism, allowing a speaker to vent or explore deeper feelings they might not otherwise address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify jokes that ease tension between audience and performer or about a stressful/tragic subject; relief theory accounts for finding humor in otherwise unfunny situations (e.g., laugh as release; laughter when tickled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Superiority theory suggests humor relies on ridicule, derision, or put-downs that raise the speaker by drawing attention to the weaknesses or infirmities of a target (includes self-deprecating humor as a variant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code jokes that position the comedian on a moral/high ground or that elevate the comedian relative to an out-group; ensure the target is established as inferior via explicit or implicit in-group/out-group cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity theory relies on contradictions and incongruences in content and/or delivery, subverting expectations and revealing something different than the audience was led to believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify setups that present one framing and then reveal an unexpected resolution or contradiction; focus on the initial realization of incongruity and how it is resolved in the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple classical-theory labels per joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern approaches synthesize the three classical theories; a single joke may utilize relief, superiority, incongruity, any combination of them, or none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding, permit jokes to be categorized into more than one theory; expect overlaps (e.g., superiority and incongruity often co-occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Building rapport (persuasive strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can build rapport with an audience, creating a positive mood that makes the audience less likely to disagree with the persuasive content and increases the comedian's likeability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code instances where the comedian establishes connection/likability (e.g., addressing the audience, working the room, opening jokes meant to predispose audience favor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic wisecracks / sarcasm (persuasive strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ironic wisecracks and sarcasm can distract from or discredit potential counterarguments to the comedian's positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark jokes that use sarcasm or cutting irony to undercut opposing viewpoints; the study notes this as the most-used persuasive method (e.g., Buress uses ironic wisecracks in ~90% of jokes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-effacing humor (persuasive strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-effacing humor exposes vulnerabilities and can improve the speaker's credibility by suggesting honesty and relatability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code jokes where the comedian is the butt of the joke to increase audience identification and perceived candor; track changes in frequency over time as a measure of rapport/relatability strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nabi's guidance for persuasive humorous messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous persuasive messages are double-edged: naturalistic, conversational contexts increase persuasive effectiveness, but humor risks being dismissed as 'just a joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To counteract discounting, conclude the humorous message by reestablishing serious intent; expect that humorous messages may reduce counterargument and enhance perceived argument quality, and may influence attitudes after a delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charged humor: definition and deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Charged humor challenges social inequality and cultural exclusion; it 'unmasks inequality by identifying legal arrangements and cultural attitudes contributing to subordinated status.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy charged humor sparingly to maintain mainstream success; the tactic of 'throw in a charged zinger here and there' is recommended over making an entire show charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding unit: use of album track lists to define jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes (bits) were drawn from album track lists, as those distinctions are pre-determined by the performer; when a track list is unavailable (e.g., streaming-only special), the researcher uses verbal cues and prior formatting to segment material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the performer's published track divisions as the authoritative unit boundary; when forced to segment, follow verbal segues and consistent conventions to approximate album-style divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding procedure and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should be coded under three lenses in order: (1) which classical theories the joke utilized, (2) which persuasive strategies (per Lyttle) were present, and (3) its sociopolitical subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three coding lenses to each joke; allow multiple codes per lens (e.g., a joke can employ multiple theories and multiple persuasive strategies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociopolitical thematic categories for coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Thematic categories used in coding include: race relations; sex/gender/relationships; defiance of authority/police; American politics; violence; drugs/alcohol; defiance of social norms/etiquette; applying social norms to the absurd; religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories may emerge naturally and require iterative recoding of earlier material when new categories appear; record counts of jokes per category and overlaps across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative metrics to report
rubrics_metrics.description: Report counts and percentages of jokes by theory, by persuasive strategy, by theme, and report overlaps (e.g., number of jokes employing two or three theories/strategies; distribution of how many themes per joke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tables (cross-tabs) showing frequencies and percentages, and highlight prominent overlaps (e.g., how many jokes use all three theories) to substantiate claims about predominant methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic style and persona features to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether material relies on storytelling jokes vs direct addressing of social issues, the performer's delivery (e.g., 'bemusement, skepticism, made-you-think discomfort'), and the writerly approach (e.g., observational/procedural joke-writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess delivery cadence, frequency and placement of rapport-building, and the balance of storytelling versus explicit political critique as part of the performer's persona analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/chronological analysis for career trajectory
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze material in chronological order (when possible) to examine development of onstage persona, craft, and thematic shifts over time; exceptions (e.g., a viral clip) may be evaluated separately first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare earlier to later specials to detect shifts in prevalence of persuasive strategies, sociopolitical content, and use of self-effacing humor or rapport-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/impact considerations and audience call-to-action
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can influence public opinion and spur real-world consequences; a comedian may explicitly urge audiences to research claims to reestablish seriousness (as Buress did regarding Cosby).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating persuasive impact, consider downstream effects (e.g., virality, media attention, accusers stepping forward) and whether the comedian signals seriousness to overcome the 'just a joke' dismissal.
